children: 0813 ET - A more stable job outlook is keeping U.S. consumers afloat for the time being, TD Securities analysts say. Consumers are still feeling strapped for cash due to high prices, but their position is less dire than last year, the analysts say. That's because private payrolls are strong and the unemployment rate has come back down from hitting 4.5% in November 2025, the analysts say. Youth labor market conditions, which were a source of concern last year, have improved in 2026, they say. (katherine.hamilton@wsj.com)

0727 ET - While an interest-rate hike by the European Central Bank next week seems likely, further tightening could pose growing risks to the eurozone economy, ING's Carsten Brzeski says in a note. The risk is heightened by surging bond yields, which are tightening financing conditions and putting pressure on public finances, he says. Higher bond yields can have an even greater impact on growth and inflation than equivalent policy-rate increases, Brzeski notes. With inflation largely driven by elevated energy prices rather than overheating demand, additional hikes would do little to address the underlying supply shock while increasing the danger of unnecessarily restrictive policy. "It's difficult to envisage the ECB being willing to risk a recession to tackle what is still a textbook supply-side shock." (don.forbes@wsj.com)

0722 ET - The continued climb in gas prices amid escalating U.S.-Iran tensions and the increase in eurozone inflation to 3.3% in August cement a September rate hike from the European Central Bank, Ebury's Matthew Ryan says. Even so, a passthrough from the energy spike to underlying inflation was still conspicuously absent in August's data, he says. Core inflation declined to 2.4% from 2.5% in July, returning to its February level before the start of the Iran war. "While a September hike looks all but guaranteed, further tightening into restrictive territory beyond that is far from certain." That could keep a lid on further appreciation of the euro against the dollar, particularly given how aggressively markets are currently pricing in additional hikes, Ryan says. (edward.frankl@wsj.com)

0720 ET - Markets increase their expectations of the Bank of England increasing interest rates in the coming months as oil prices surge. Brent crude oil last trades at $94.32 a barrel, notably higher than last week's levels, after the U.S. and Iran resumed hostilities over the weekend. Investors currently fully price in two quarter-point BOE rate rises by February 2027, and a potential third one by June, LSEG data show. Last week, markets were only fully pricing two BOE rate hikes by the end of 2027. (miriam.mukuru@wsj.com)

0715 ET - Yields on U.K. sovereign bonds, also referred to as gilts, could stay elevated given high energy costs due to Middle East tensions, Aberdeen Investments' Matthew Amis says in a note. Ten-year gilt yields hit a 19-year high of 5.294% on Wednesday while 30-year yields increase to 5.921%, their highest since 1998, LSEG data show. High government borrowing costs will weigh on public finances, Amis says. "With gilt yields at these levels, the fiscal room for manoeuvre going into October's budget is incredibly limited." The U.K. budget is due on Oct. 28. (miriam.mukuru@wsj.com)

0646 ET - The yen got a little lift from BOJ hawk Takata's comments, but a hawkish Fed is a game-changer that suggests the currency can spend much longer in the 160-162 area against the dollar, says ING's Chris Turner. The implication that the BOJ could hike by 50 bps or deliver back-to-back increases sounds positive for the yen, though Turner notes that Takata is in the minority hawk camp and his comments shouldn't be particularly surprising. A September hike would already represent quicker tightening, and ING suspects the BOJ would prefer to wait until 2027 to see how domestic consumption performs. Turner reckons Treasury Secretary Bessent won't be particularly happy with the hawkish Fed working against the yen, but will appreciate the benefits of Fed independence. (fabiana.negrinochoa@wsj.com)

0623 ET - Treasury yields continue to rise, with the 10-year yield hitting near three-year high, while the dollar reaches its highest in nearly three weeks as rising oil prices add to expectations for higher U.S. interest rates. "Federal Reserve Governor Michael Barr stated that he would support an interest-rate hike should inflation fail to moderate," Exness' Christopher Tahir says in a note. More comments like this from other Fed officials could further bolster yields and the currency, the strategist says. Middle East tensions add to this narrative, reviving inflation concerns, he says. The DXY dollar index rises to a high of 99.847. The 10-year Treasury yield reaches 4.818%, according to LSEG. (emese.bartha@wsj.com)

0612 ET - The current sharp increase in U.K. government bond yields, or gilt yields, raises the risk of new tax rises at this year's budget on Oct. 28, Ebury's Matthew Ryan says in a note. Ten-year yields hit 5.294% on Wednesday, a 19-year high, LSEG data show. Thirty-year gilt yields climb to 5.921%, their highest since 1998. "This rise in yields, which will eat directly into the government's fiscal headroom, raises the risk of tax hikes in the autumn," he says. (miriam.mukuru@wsj.com)

0600 ET - Beijing might favor a gradual yuan appreciation, according to Goldman Sachs in a note. Beijing's stated economic policy objectives include further growth in high-tech sectors to "build a manufacturing superpower" and "self-reliance" in key inputs and technologies, and increased internationalization of the renminbi, GS says. "We anticipate China's policymakers will continue to favor gradual Chinese yuan appreciation against the U.S. dollar (3-5%/year) as the option that best balances these objectives," GS says. (tracy.qu@wsj.com)

0558 ET - Asia high-yield credit continues to be a compelling opportunity in the region, says John Li at J.P. Morgan Private Bank. After a record default wave, Li says the asset class has turned a corner. Total 1H returns are approaching 4% and defaults are close to zero year-to-date. Yields remain attractive, while stronger corporate balance sheets and a more supportive refinancing backdrop should help keep defaults contained. Asia HY could also benefit from renewed investor interest in emerging-market debt. Asia credit as a whole enters 2H on solid footing after outperforming broader fixed-income markets in 1H, with carry likely to be the dominant driver of returns in a higher-for-longer rates environment. "Over the next 12 months, we expect total returns of approximately 5.0%-5.5% for Asia IG and 7%-8% for Asia HY." (fabiana.negrinochoa@wsj.com)

0535 ET - Yields on U.K. government bonds, or gilts, are at multi-year highs, adding pressure to already stretched public finances, Handelsbanken's senior U.K. economist Daniel Mahoney says in a note. "Current moves in financial markets are clearly set to further erode the government's fiscal headroom at the upcoming budget," he says. Elevated borrowing costs raise the risk of new tax rises at the budget next month, Mahoney says. Nonetheless, if Middle East tensions ease, this could enable gilt yields to fall, he says. Ten-year gilt yields rise 8 basis points to last trade at 5.285%, having hit a 19-year high of 5.294%, LSEG data show. Thirty-year gilt yields rise to 5.921%, their highest since 1998. (miriam.mukuru@wsj.com)

0449 ET - The oil market is increasingly pricing the cost of an unresolved war, Phillip Nova'a Priyanka Sachdeva says in a note. The latest disruption is no longer limited to military escalation, as reports of attacks on vessels passing through the Strait of Hormuz bring the risk directly into the physical oil supply chain, the analyst notes. The most feasible outcome now looks like stretched negotiations and prolonged trouble for oil flows, rather than a quick resolution, she says. The longer the disruption continues, the greater the risk that higher crude prices become embedded into inflation expectations and eventually into monetary policy decisions, Sachdeva adds. (sherry.qin@wsj.com)
